intro: The Metropolitan Park of Santiago is the largest urban park in Chile, and its hills hold the geological history of the city. GEOPARQUEMET is a project of the Geoheritage Unit of Sernageomin (the Chilean National Geology and Mining Service) to identify, record and promote the geodiversity and geosites of the park.

To tell you that story we have chosen a few significant places, which we call geosites, that reflect the most important or unusual processes that gave rise to these hills and to the landscape of our city. These geosites are grouped into georoutes that you can walk in the park or explore virtually.

Geo-Route 1 links the Pío Nono entrance with the Tupahue swimming pool. Along almost three kilometers you will discover 28-million-year-old volcanic rocks, 21-million-year-old intrusive rocks, and the processes that transform them into the soil beneath our feet.
aviso: Walk on sidewalks and footpaths, bring water and sunscreen, and keep away from the rock walls: blocks may fall.

1.cap: The cracks in the rock are highlighted with blue lines and with yellow, red and blue surfaces.
texto: The oldest rocks of San Cristóbal Hill, like the ones we see at this geosite, formed during several explosive [[erupcion-volcanica|volcanic eruptions]] 28 million years ago. After being buried, these rocks were affected by forces caused by the movement of the [[placas-tectonicas|tectonic plates]], which not only pushed them but also deformed and fractured them. When the rocks reached the surface again, the cracks tended to open and split the rock mass into blocks of different sizes, helped by the action of the [[agentes-atmosfericos|atmospheric agents]] that affect rock at the surface.

The fractures we can see in the rocks of this geosite, and the rock blocks they create, formed through the process described above. To highlight them, yellow, red and blue surfaces and blue lines were painted on the image of this rock wall. The painted surfaces show cracks with different orientations in space, which is why we see them at different angles and directions on the rock wall. Because of this orientation, unstable rock blocks form in the wall; due to their shape they are called “wedges”.

Pulled by gravity, the blocks can slide and fall, piling up at the side of the road. This can be dangerous for visitors, so it is best to keep away from these walls and walk only in the areas marked for pedestrians.
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] we can see the cracks in 28-million-year-old [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] and the blocks these fractures create.

2.cap: Dike, marked in yellow, hosted in volcanic rocks (blue).
texto: Rocks almost always have cracks, whose openings and lengths can vary a lot. These fractures allow different fluids and gases to flow through them. About 21 million years ago, the same [[magma|magma]] that fed the volcanic eruptions in this area also flowed into and filled the fractures of the rock below the surface. Its later cooling at depth produced what we call [[rocas-intrusivas|intrusive rocks]].

At this geosite you can see the result of that process: an intrusive rock (highlighted in yellow) that formed from molten rock (magma) that entered and cooled inside a fracture (highlighted with red lines) of an older volcanic rock (painted blue). Because of its shape and orientation, this rock body is called a [[dique|dike]].
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] you can see a body of intrusive rock hosted within [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]]. Because of its shape and orientation, this rock body is called a [[dique|dike]] (highlighted in yellow and marked with the letter B). It formed from molten rock ([[magma|magma]]) that entered and cooled inside a fracture (highlighted with red lines) of an older volcanic rock (painted violet and marked with the letter A).

In this image, the volcanic rock marked with the letter A looks much more uniform and resistant than the volcanic rock marked with the letter C. The rock in this lower area was probably more fractured to begin with than the upper zone (A), so that while the [[magma|magma]] cooled some fluids flowed mainly through it. The circulation of hot fluids transformed the minerals that originally made up the rock, replacing them with others that make these pieces of stone much weaker than the original rock. These same fluids also produced the whitish minerals that filled the cracks and give this area its mosaic look.

3.cap: Blue lines mark some of the fractures, and the roots that have grown into them are highlighted in green. Yellow shows the mineral filling found in some of them.
texto: When rocks are exposed at the surface, [[agentes-atmosfericos|atmospheric agents]] (temperature, humidity), water and biological activity cause different changes in them. These physical, chemical and mineralogical transformations gradually weaken, break and turn them into other materials, which eventually give rise to soil: the outermost layer of the Earth's crust, the skin of the rocks.

As the [[suelo|soil]]-forming processes, which together are called [[meteorizacion|weathering]], reach deeper, different layers form, one on top of the other, each with its own characteristics. Two levels can be clearly seen here: the uppermost soil, shown in red in one of the images, where the rock is almost completely broken down and rich in organic matter. Herbs and shrubs take root in this layer. The second layer, beneath the first, is rock much less affected by soil-forming processes. Although it has lost much of its strength, it still keeps its original structures. Even the fractures in the rock can still be recognized.
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] you can see different layers of [[suelo|soil]] formed from the breakdown of rocks. Two levels can be clearly seen here: the uppermost [[suelo|soil]], shown in red in the image, where the rock is almost completely broken down and rich in organic matter.

And it is these cracks, formed millions of years ago deep inside the Earth, that open at the surface and let trees sink their roots. In the image, blue lines mark some fractures, while the exposed surface of others has been painted violet. The roots that have grown into these fractures are highlighted in green. Yellow shows the filling found in some of them, made of minerals deposited by circulating fluids. The whitish crystals are mostly [[carbonato-de-calcio|calcium carbonate]], the same mineral that builds up inside kettles and in the pipes of our homes.

4.cap: At this geosite you can see pyroxene crystals in intrusive rock.
texto: About 21 million years ago, several volcanoes were erupting in the Santiago area. The products of this activity were deposited on top of the park's oldest volcanic rocks (28 million years old), but we cannot see them today because they were completely eroded between 10 and 5 million years ago. The only evidence of that volcanism, seen at this geosite, is the rocks that formed at depth when the magma cooled, both in the feeder conduits of the volcanoes or their magma chambers and in the fractures of the older rock (see Geosite 2).
There, the magma cools slowly and its components crystallize, forming what we call intrusive rocks.

Because of where and how fast they cool, these rocks look very different from the volcanic rocks around them. Even so, we can also see fractures in them similar to those in the other rocks; in the photograph they are marked with blue lines to highlight them.

One of the main features of these rocks is that they are made entirely of crystals. Although these are usually very small, at this geosite some of them can be several centimeters long on their longest side. This is the case of a mineral called [[piroxeno|pyroxene]], whose crystals stand out in the rock because of their dark color and more or less rectangular shapes. In the images, which are field photographs and hand samples, they are painted green to make them stand out even more.
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] we can see [[rocas-intrusivas|intrusive rocks]], probably formed 21 million years ago in the feeder conduits of volcanoes or in their magma chambers.
Because of their origin, these rocks look very different from the [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] around them.

5.cap: Layered breakdown (green) of intrusive rocks. Unweathered rock cores are marked with red circles.
texto: When rocks are exposed at the surface, atmospheric agents (temperature, humidity), water and biological activity cause different changes in them. These physical, chemical and mineralogical transformations gradually weaken, break and turn them into other materials. Water is one of the main agents that modify the materials that make up rocks. It also takes advantage of the cracks present in most rocks to concentrate its action and extend it to depth.

What we can see at this geosite is precisely the result of the processes described in the previous paragraph. The action of water and the transforming processes, which started and were at first concentrated along the cracks of the rocks (marked in blue in the photo), attacked the blocks from their edges. As they advanced inward, they produced a series of sheets, like the layers of an onion (painted green in the photo), that wrap around a more or less rounded core of rock marked with a red line in the images. In geology this process is called “[[meteorizacion-esferoidal|spheroidal weathering]]”.
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] we can see the result of the processes that weaken and break down an intrusive rock, and the structures they create.

The action of water and the transforming processes, which started and were at first concentrated along the cracks of the rocks (marked in blue in the photo), attacked the blocks from their edges. As they advanced inward, they produced a series of sheets, like the layers of an onion (painted green in the photo), that wrap around a more or less rounded core of rock marked with a red line in this image.
This process also gives the rock walls their appearance: countless rounded blocks, marked in red in the images, isolated between concentric layers of rock a few centimeters thick.

6.titulo: Contact between volcanic and intrusive rock
6.cap: Contact zone between volcanic rocks and intrusive rocks.
texto: The oldest rocks of San Cristóbal Hill, like those we see at this geosite and that are painted red in the images, formed during successive explosive volcanic eruptions. Seven million years later, magmatic activity continued in more or less the same place, and several volcanoes were erupting at the same time in the Santiago area. The products of this activity were deposited on top of the older volcanic rocks, but we cannot see them today because they were completely eroded between 10 and 5 million years ago.

The only evidence of that volcanism is the rocks that formed at depth when the magma cooled. So the intrusive rocks we see at this geosite, painted green in the images, may have formed in the roots of some of those ancient volcanoes, in this case in their feeder conduits or their [[camara-volcanica-o-magmatica|magma chambers]].
texto_web: At this [[geositio|geosite]] we can see very clearly the zone where the park's oldest [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]], about 28 million years old, meet the [[rocas-intrusivas|intrusive rocks]], about 21 million years old.
The [[rocas-intrusivas|intrusive rocks]], painted green in the images, may have formed in the roots of some ancient volcanoes (21 million years ago), in their feeder conduits or their magma chambers.

7.cap: Welded tuff where some flattened volcanic fragments, called fiamme, can be clearly seen (highlighted in orange).
texto: The oldest rocks of San Cristóbal Hill, like the ones we see at this geosite, formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions. These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out gases, ash and glowing fragments of rock.

After falling back to the ground, this material is compressed by its own weight (or by the weight of other layers piled on top of it) and cools, forming rocks called [[toba-volcanica|tuffs]]. When the fragments of molten rock land while still hot and soft, compaction deforms and flattens them, and the heat and pressure also weld them together, forming what we call “welded tuffs”.
texto_web: These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out [[magma|magma]], gases and rock fragments. When the fragments of [[magma|magma]] land while still hot and soft, compaction deforms and flattens them, and the heat and pressure also weld them together, forming what we call “welded tuffs”.

At this [[geositio|geosite]] we can see a welded tuff with some clearly flattened volcanic fragments. Known in geology as fiamme, they take on lens-like shapes that here reach up to 20 cm long. In this image they are painted orange to make them stand out a little more from the rock that contains them.

8.titulo: The rock of the Tupahue pool
8.cap: The rock set in the pool is split into two blocks of different sizes, with flat faces that are cracks (fractures), marked with blue lines. Most of them have a reddish coating of oxidized iron minerals, and a whitish layer of calcium carbonate is deposited on the part under water.
texto: The rocks of the Tupahue pool are volcanic in origin and, because of their features, are called “welded tuff”. That is, during an explosive eruption the fragments of molten rock thrown out by the volcano landed while still hot and soft. The compaction of all this material deformed and flattened some of the still-hot fragments, which took on lens-like shapes, just as you can see at Geosite 7.

In this rock you can also find pieces of crystals, mainly of a mineral called [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]], painted yellow in the image, and pieces of older volcanic rock, painted violet to highlight them.
texto_web: The Tupahue pool opened in 1966 and has operated continuously ever since. It was built where an old quarry used to be which, in the early 1960s, had turned into a large rubbish dump.

The architect in charge of the pool laid out its design on site and did not originally include the rock we see inside it today. It was found at the bottom of the old quarry after the loose material left by the rock extraction was cleared away. Because of its beauty and size, the architect decided to change the original design and include the rock in the pool, making it part of the leisure and enjoyment this pool offers.

In 2015, by Decree No. 536, the mural of the Tupahue pool was declared a Historic Monument, and the same decree declared the area around the mural a Typical Zone, which includes the pool and its rock.

d: All the processes that take place in the atmosphere, the layer of gases around the Earth, and that transform rocks and shape the landscape. They include precipitation (rain, snow), wind, temperature and air humidity.

The cavity beneath the surface of a [[volcan|volcano]] where [[magma|magma]] is stored before being expelled to the surface as a [[erupcion-volcanica|volcanic eruption]]. The chamber connects to the crater of the [[volcan|volcano]] through a conduit known as the vent. Various physical and chemical processes can take place inside it, such as the interaction of the [[magma|magma]] with the surrounding rock and the crystallization of minerals.

Calcium carbonate is a chemical compound made of carbon, oxygen and calcium. In nature it occurs in rocks as the minerals calcite and aragonite. It is the main component of limestone and of marble, which forms from limestone through a process called metamorphism. It is also found in living organisms, mainly in their shells and skeletons. It is very often dissolved in water, and when its content is high we speak of “hard water”. Its presence in your city's water shows up as the scale left in kettles, taps and pipes, which forms when this compound precipitates.
An opening or crack, usually at the top of a [[volcan|volcano]], through which solid, liquid and gaseous materials are expelled from inside the Earth.

An intrusive rock formed from [[magma|magma]] that fills and cools inside a pre-existing crack in another rock. It is therefore much younger than the rock that contains it. It is shaped like a slab, with a thickness from centimeters to a couple of meters, much smaller than its length, which can reach kilometers.

The Eocene is a division of the geological time scale that lasted from about 56 to 34 million years ago. Its name comes from the Greek words eos, ‘dawn’, and kainos, ‘new’, referring to the first appearance of modern fauna. During this epoch some of the world's most important mountain ranges formed, such as the Alps and the Himalayas, and there were several major climate changes. At the start of the Eocene the climate was hot and humid, and the Earth was almost entirely covered by forests. Then global cooling began, bringing marked seasons. As a result, deciduous trees (which lose their leaves in autumn and winter) began to prevail over tropical evergreen species, since they were better adapted to large temperature changes. Birds dominated over other fauna and the first cetaceans began to develop. There was also a great expansion and diversification of ants. A mass extinction, especially of mammals, known as the Grande Coupure (great break), marks the end of the Eocene.

The process by which rocks and sediments are worn away by water, wind or ice, and the loosened material is carried away by these same agents. It changes the land surface, both by wearing down rocks and by piling the material up somewhere else.

The expulsion of [[magma|magma]], volcanic gases and rock fragments from the crater of a [[volcan|volcano]] or from a volcanic fissure. It can be calm (effusive) or violent (explosive), depending on several factors, including the composition of the [[magma|magma]], its gas content and its interaction with water or ice. A volcanic eruption is a natural phenomenon that can become a disaster when the [[volcan|volcano]] is close to where people live.

The different stages of Earth's history recorded in the rocks are represented in the Geological Time Scale. One of the major divisions in our planet's geological history is the start of the Cambrian period (and of the Paleozoic era), when the fossil record becomes very abundant and diverse and includes representatives of most known animal phyla. Because of the contrast with the life that came before, two major divisions of geological time are recognized: the Precambrian eon and the Phanerozoic eon (meaning ‘visible life’). Eons are divided into “eras”, and eras into “periods”. The two smaller subdivisions are “epochs” (some of them described in this glossary) and “ages”. All divisions are based on major changes in past life forms preserved in the rocks. Fossils therefore let us determine the relative age (ages, epochs, periods, etc.) of the rocks that contain them (mainly sedimentary rocks). Radiometric dating carried out in specialized laboratories, based on the half-life of certain radioactive elements in the rocks, tells us their numerical ages. In this way the geological time scale is constantly refined as knowledge and technology advance.

The name given to cone-shaped volcanoes (the most typical and familiar volcano shape). They are built up by successive eruptions of [[lava|lava]] and other volcanic products expelled by the [[volcan|volcano]] as it evolves and grows.

A geological fault is a fracture in rocks along which the blocks on either side move relative to each other. Faults and the movement of the blocks are caused by the forces that drive the motion of the [[placas-tectonicas|tectonic plates]]. There are several types of faults depending on the direction in which the blocks move.

A sequence of layers of [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] and [[rocas-sedimentarias|sedimentary rocks]] found in the Andes and in the isolated hills of the Metropolitan and O’Higgins regions. It was defined in 1960 by Luis Aguirre and redefined in this area by Wall, Sellés and Gana in 1999. Its layers are strongly deformed and reach visible thicknesses of up to 2 km. Radiometric dating in the area gives ages between 34 and 20 million years, placing it at the end of the [[eoceno|Eocene]] and the beginning of the [[mioceno|Miocene]].

The main formal unit in the classification of rock layers. Formations are defined by their own characteristics and by their position in space and time relative to the surrounding units. They must be large enough to be drawn on a map and can range from less than a meter to kilometers thick.

When [[lava|lava]] cools at the surface, or [[magma|magma]] cools inside the Earth, cracks form where the hot material touches the air, the ground or the surrounding rock, because the [[magma|magma]] or [[lava|lava]] contracts as it cools. These cracks spread into the hot body as it cools and, as they advance, arrange themselves into column shapes. The columns, whose ends have 3 to 8 sides, can be several meters long and up to about 4 m across, and they stand perpendicular to the cooling surface. Structures like these can be seen in Parquemet and on Santa Lucía Hill in Santiago.

Geodiversity is the variety of natural elements in an area that are the product and record of the planet's history and evolution there. They include rocks, minerals, sediments, soils, fossils, meteorites, outcrops, structures, landscapes and landforms that let us learn about, study and interpret the processes that have shaped the planet and that, together, form the ground on which life and societies develop.
A set of geosites arranged to form a route that can be followed on foot or by other means, showing the highlights of the [[geodiversidad|geodiversity]] of the area.

A geosite is a specific place where one or more elements of [[geodiversidad|geodiversity]] are present, with outstanding or unusual features that give it high value for one or more of the following: the study and knowledge of the Earth sciences, education in those disciplines, recreation, or cultural expression.

The Holocene is a division of the geological time scale that runs from 11,700 years ago to the present. It is the most recent geological epoch, although some scientists propose a new epoch called the “Anthropocene”, marked by humanity's influence on geological processes and the loss of biodiversity. Its name comes from the Greek words holos, ‘whole’, and kainos, ‘new’ or ‘recent’. The Holocene follows the [[pleistoceno|Pleistocene]], an epoch of great glaciations that affected the whole planet. The Holocene climate is therefore marked by rising temperatures and gradual deglaciation at all latitudes, with some colder periods such as the so-called “Little Ice Age” (around 1300 AD). Plants and animals have not evolved greatly during this epoch; it is marked instead by loss of biodiversity and the extinction of many species, which continues today. Homo sapiens is the only human species that has lived in this epoch, developing great civilizations whose growth and activities have had a strong impact on the environment.

The word lava comes from Italian and derives from the Latin labes, meaning ‘fall’, slope or to penetrate. It refers to the molten, glowing rock that flows out of the crater or a fissure of a [[volcan|volcano]] during an eruption and runs down its slopes. Lava temperatures range from 700 °C to 1,200 °C, and lava can flow as slowly as 1 km a day or as fast as 10 km an hour, depending on its chemical composition. Before a [[volcan|volcano]] expels it, the molten material inside the Earth is called [[magma|magma]]. Geologists also call the rocks that form when this molten material cools lavas.

Two or more crystals of the same mineral that grow together following a defined symmetry relationship, so that one looks like the mirror image or a rotation of the other. It is very common in feldspars such as [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]].
Molten rock material, a mixture of gases, liquids and crystals, that forms inside the Earth and can be expelled to the surface during volcanic eruptions.

A particular way in which rocks break down, caused by chemical processes followed by physical forces that peel the rock into thin concentric layers around a more or less rounded core. Water breaks down certain minerals, producing iron oxides and clay minerals. Because these take up more volume than the original minerals, they create forces that eventually split the rock into thin layers.
The transformation of rocks at or near the surface through physical disintegration (breaking into pieces) and chemical alteration (decomposition).

The Miocene is a division of the geological time scale that lasted from about 23 to 5 million years ago. Its name comes from the Greek words meion, ‘less’, and kainos, ‘new’, because it has 18% fewer modern marine invertebrates than the [[plioceno|Pliocene]], the epoch that followed. At the start of the Miocene the climate was relatively warm, but from about 16 to 8 million years ago temperatures fell and the Antarctic ice sheets formed. Plants and animals of this epoch were fairly modern. Mammals and birds were well established, and primitive forms of the rhinoceros, cat, camel and horse already existed. Great apes lived in southern Europe, Africa and Asia, and the first hominids began to evolve in East Africa. In the seas, whales, dolphins, sharks and seals developed and spread.

The Oligocene is a division of the geological time scale that lasted from about 34 to 23 million years ago. Its name comes from the Greek oligos, ‘few’, and kainos, ‘recent’, referring to the scarcity of new modern mammals after their rapid and widespread evolution in the [[eoceno|Eocene]], the previous epoch. The Oligocene is marked by the rise of mammals as the dominant form of land life and by the start of a global cooling trend that would culminate in the glacial periods of the [[pleistoceno|Pleistocene]]. The first elephants with trunks, the first horses and a great variety of grasses appeared in this epoch.

Pyroxenes are a group of minerals that form in igneous and metamorphic rocks under high pressure and temperature (1,000 to 1,300 °C). Their name comes from the ancient Greek words pyr and xenos, meaning “fire” and “stranger”. They are made of single chains of silica tetrahedra linked by cations of iron, calcium, magnesium and aluminum, among others. Iron-bearing pyroxenes are dark, while those without iron tend to be whitish, gray or light green. They form prisms or small needles.

The different blocks into which the Earth's outer layer is divided. They are rigid blocks of varying thickness and size that slide over a more viscous material called the “asthenosphere”, part of the planet's upper mantle. Together, all the tectonic plates form a jigsaw puzzle of many pieces that interact in different ways. Chile lies on the boundary between two plates, one sinking beneath the other, and their movements cause the earthquakes we feel from time to time.

Plagioclases are a group of minerals that, together with others, belong to the feldspars. Feldspars are the most abundant minerals in the Earth's crust, and plagioclases alone make up about 40% of the volume of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Their name comes from the ancient Greek words πλάγιος and κλάσις, meaning “oblique” and “fracture”. Plagioclases form a continuous series of minerals whose composition ranges from albite (containing only sodium) to anorthite (containing only calcium), the names of the plagioclases at either end of the series. They are usually white or light gray, with prismatic or tabular shapes.

The Pleistocene is a division of the geological time scale that lasted from about 2.6 million to 11,700 years ago. Its name comes from the Greek words pleistos, ‘most’, and kainos, ‘new’, referring to the appearance of the most modern fauna. This epoch saw a series of at least five glaciations, alternating with somewhat warmer periods, which is why it is known as the “Ice Age”. At least 30% of the planet's surface is thought to have been covered by glacial ice and, because of low rainfall and the storage of water in polar and other ice, sea level fell at least 100 m below today's level. By this time the continents were already in their present position. The Pleistocene was the first epoch in which Homo sapiens appeared and, by its end, humans had spread across the whole planet, using the land and ice bridges left by the glaciations and the low sea level. Megafauna and the dominance of mammals are typical of this epoch. However, the mammoth, the mastodon, the cave bear, the saber-toothed cat and other large mammals of that time died out towards its end, mainly in North and South America (73% of large mammals and 80% of mammal genera respectively). Other smaller mammals that survived this great extinction can still be recognized today. The San Vicente de Tagua-Tagua lagoon, in the O’Higgins Region, is the place in Chile where the largest number of species from that epoch has been found, while in Pilauco, in the city of Osorno, Los Lagos Region, a site museum displays its huge and significant paleontological record.

The Pliocene is a division of the geological time scale that lasted from about 5 to 2.5 million years ago. Its name comes from the Greek words pleion, ‘more’, and kainos, ‘new’, referring to the spread of modern fauna, mainly mammals. The Pliocene climate changed from warm to cold, with marked seasons towards its end, and the cooling continued into the [[pleistoceno|Pleistocene]] and its successive glaciations. During the Pliocene the Isthmus of Panama formed, separating the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and cutting off the warm equatorial currents. As a result both oceans cooled, especially Arctic and Antarctic waters. The colder, drier climate reduced tropical plants to a narrow equatorial belt, and with very marked seasons deciduous trees increased. Land and marine fauna were essentially modern, although land animals looked somewhat more primitive than today's. The first recognizable hominid, Australopithecus, appeared in Africa in this epoch, along with other hominid species such as Homo habilis and Homo erectus, considered direct ancestors of Homo sapiens.

Intrusive rocks (also called plutonic rocks) form when [[magma|magma]] cools and solidifies inside the Earth. They are igneous rocks (from the Latin ignis, meaning fire), a category they share with extrusive or volcanic igneous rocks, which, unlike intrusive rocks, form when [[magma|magma]] cools and solidifies at the surface. There are several criteria for classifying an intrusive rock, each with its own purpose, such as how the rocks occur, crystal size, mineral content or chemical composition.

Sedimentary rocks form from transported fragments of existing rocks, from the chemical precipitation of certain elements and compounds (limestone, for example, which is used to make cement), or from the accumulation of organic matter (the coal once mined in Lota is an example). About 75% of the rocks we see at the Earth's surface are sedimentary.

Volcanic rocks form when [[magma|magma]] cools and solidifies after being expelled to the surface during a [[erupcion-volcanica|volcanic eruption]]. They are igneous rocks (from the Latin ignis, meaning fire), a category they share with intrusive igneous rocks, which, unlike volcanic rocks, form when [[magma|magma]] cools and solidifies inside the Earth.

Soil is the outermost, visible part of the continents. It is where we grow crops, build our homes and bury our dead. It is a thin, extremely varied layer made of minerals, organic matter, tiny plants and animals, air and water. Soil [[formacion|formation]] is a very slow process: it takes several centuries for soil to reach the minimum thickness needed for most crops. The process begins with the breakdown of surface rocks by water, temperature changes and wind. Then microorganisms decompose the plants and animals that grow and die in and on the soil, turning them into organic matter that mixes with it. In this way soil-forming processes reach deeper and create different layers, each with its own characteristics.

Also called a marine terrace, it is a more or less flat, horizontal surface found along the coast at different heights above sea level. It is formed by marine [[erosion|erosion]] of the coast and is usually covered by sediments. Sometimes there is more than one terrace, arranged like steps along the coast. This landform owes its position above sea level to two different processes: changes in sea level, or uplift caused by tectonic forces.

The material produced by violent volcanic eruptions and later piled up on the ground surface. These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments. After falling back under gravity, this material is compressed by its own weight (or by other layers on top of it) and cools, forming the rocks called tuffs. When the fragments of molten rock land while still hot and soft, compaction deforms and flattens them, and heat and pressure also weld them together, forming what are called “welded tuffs”.

A unit of [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] found in Parquemet. About 28 to 25 million years old ([[oligoceno|Oligocene]]), these rocks have been assigned to the [[formacion-abanico|Abanico Formation]]. Grayish brown to whitish brown, these rocks, called tuffs because of their features, contain pieces of crystals, mainly of the minerals [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]] and [[piroxeno|pyroxene]], and pieces of older [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] and intrusive rocks up to 60 cm on their longest side. In some places flattened pieces of volcanic glass (fiamme) can also be seen. The rocks of Cerro Blanco formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions. These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments. After falling back under gravity, this material is compressed by its own weight (or by other layers on top of it), cools and solidifies.

A unit of [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] found in Parquemet. About 26 to 23 million years old ([[oligoceno|Oligocene]]), these rocks have been assigned to the [[formacion-abanico|Abanico Formation]]. The unit is divided into two subunits. Subunit 1 is found on the lower part of the ridge immediately north of the La Pirámide area and consists mainly of tuff-type rocks, similar to those of the [[unidad-cerro-san-cristobal|Cerro San Cristóbal Unit]], with volcanic breccias and lavas in some places. These rocks contain pieces of crystals, mainly of the mineral [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]], and pieces of older [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]]. The rocks of this subunit formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions. These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments. After falling back under gravity, this material is compressed by its own weight (or by other layers on top of it), cools and solidifies. Subunit 2 is found from the middle to the summit of Cerro El Carbón. It consists mainly of lavas with very few volcanic breccias. The lavas have crystals visible to the naked eye within a more or less uniform rock mass in which no minerals can be seen without magnification. The visible minerals are mainly [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]] and [[piroxeno|pyroxene]]. These lavas also contain amygdules: cavities left in the lava by escaping gases which, after the rocks were buried, were filled by growing minerals such as calcite. The rocks of this subunit formed during successive volcanic eruptions dominated by the outflow of [[lava|lava]] from a vent that may have been located a little to the north and east of Cerro El Carbón.

A unit of [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] found in Parquemet. About 28 to 25 million years old ([[oligoceno|Oligocene]]), these rocks have been assigned to the [[formacion-abanico|Abanico Formation]]. Reddish to purplish in color, they are mainly tuffs containing pieces of crystals, most of them of the minerals [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]] and [[piroxeno|pyroxene]], as well as fragments of older [[rocas-volcanicas|volcanic rocks]] and intrusive rocks and fragments of volcanic glass (pumice). In some places, lens-shaped pumice fragments (fiamme) up to 20 cm long stand out. Rocks known as volcanic breccias can also be found, for example towards the end of the Atacameño trail, where volcanic rock fragments are more abundant and larger. The rocks of this unit, found from San Cristóbal Hill to the La Pirámide area, formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions. These eruptions produce huge explosions that throw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments. After falling back under gravity, this material is compressed by its own weight (or by other layers on top of it), cools and solidifies.

A unit of [[rocas-intrusivas|intrusive rocks]] found in Parquemet. Its rocks are made entirely of crystals, some visible to the naked eye and most of them microscopic, which form a more or less uniform grayish mass. The visible crystals are mainly the minerals [[plagioclasa|plagioclase]] and [[piroxeno|pyroxene]]. The many dikes seen in different parts of the park, such as the one at [[geositio|geosite]] 2, are related to this unit. Its rocks are found mainly on the summits of San Cristóbal, Chacarillas and Los Gemelos hills, and they formed at depth when [[magma|magma]] cooled in the feeder conduits of volcanoes or their magma chambers about 21 million years ago.

A place on the Earth's surface where [[magma|magma]], gases and pieces of rock and crystals come out from inside the Earth. These materials pile up around the volcano's crater and gradually give it its shape.

1.p: Why should you keep away from the rock walls at this geosite?
r: Cracks separate blocks (“wedges”) that can slide and fall
The rock is still hot from volcanic activity
1.e: Fractures with different orientations isolate unstable blocks called wedges. Pulled by gravity, they can slide and fall to the side of the road.

2.p: What is the dike you can see at this geosite?
r: An intrusive rock: magma that cooled inside a fracture of an older rock
A lava flow that ran over the surface
A wall built to hold back water on the hill
2.e: About 21 million years ago, magma entered a fracture in older volcanic rocks and cooled there, forming a slab-shaped body: a dike.

3.p: What is the set of processes that turns rock into soil called?
3.e: Temperature, humidity, water and biological activity weaken and break down rock at the surface. Together these processes are called weathering, and they give rise to soil.

4.p: How can you recognize the pyroxene crystals in this intrusive rock?
r: They are dark and more or less rectangular, up to several centimeters long
They are transparent like glass and rounded
They are white and form thin layers
4.e: Pyroxenes stand out because of their dark color and more or less rectangular shapes. In the images they are painted green to highlight them.

5.p: What do the sheets produced by spheroidal weathering look like?
5.e: Water attacks the blocks from their edges and creates concentric sheets, like the layers of an onion, around a sounder, rounded core of rock.

6.p: Roughly how old are the volcanic and intrusive rocks that meet here?
6.e: The oldest volcanic rocks of San Cristóbal Hill are about 28 million years old; the intrusive rocks that cut through them are about 21 million years old.

7.p: What are the flattened volcanic fragments in a welded tuff called?
7.e: Fragments of molten rock that land while still hot are flattened into lens-like shapes. Geologists call them fiamme (“flames” in Italian).

8.p: What is the whitish layer covering the underwater part of the pool rock?
r: Calcium carbonate deposited by the water, as in a kettle
Sea salt from an ancient coastline
Paint left over from building the pool
8.e: The pool water deposits calcium carbonate on the rock, through a process similar to the one that forms scale in the kettles in our homes.

Cordón Cerro San Cristóbal.desc: The volcanic rocks we see from San Cristóbal Hill to the La Pirámide area formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro El Carbón 1.desc: The volcanic rocks of this unit formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro Blanco.desc: The rocks of Cerro Blanco formed during successive very violent volcanic eruptions, with huge explosions that threw out gases, ash and glowing rock fragments.

Cerro El Carbón 2.desc: The volcanic rocks of this unit formed during successive eruptions dominated by lava flowing from a vent that may have been located a little to the north and east of Cerro El Carbón.

Pórfido andesítico.desc: The rocks of this unit formed at depth when magma cooled in the feeder conduits of volcanoes or their magma chambers, about 21 million years ago.
